criteria.dispatch_only_revoke: Put the entire lifetime inside dispatch: materialize the reply, abandon the body, and revoke in one finally for both handled and rejected requests, even though handled tokens then expire while the owner scope is still draining.
criteria.server_only_revoke: Leave dispatch doing body abandonment alone and revoke solely in the server outer finally once the per-request scope has drained; anyone calling dispatch outside a server scope takes responsibility for revoking leftover tokens or tolerates them remaining valid.
criteria.split_boundary: Share the work across layers: dispatch abandons the unread body everywhere and also revokes along rejected-route paths that never started a handler, while the server outer boundary revokes handled tokens after drainage in a finally ahead of the response return; an idempotent revoke primitive keeps the redundant coverage harmless.

revocation_boundary.instructions: How should dispatch and the server boundary divide revocation so that handled, faulted, rejected, upgraded, and unread-body requests each lose their token while admitted child work keeps working?

criteria.silent_idempotent: revokeRequest removes the token from all tables and quietly accepts unknown, forged, or previously revoked input, which keeps it safe inside finally blocks and under repeated calls for one request.
criteria.throw_unknown: revokeRequest raises the resource-state failure on unknown or previously revoked input to expose caller defects immediately, obliging each finally site to establish that its argument is still a live token.

revoke_failure_mode.instructions: How should the revokeRequest primitive react to unknown or already-revoked input?

state.lifetime_requirements: The required ordering is settled: first the handler settles and its response or upgrade outcome is materialized, next any unread live body is abandoned, then the per-request owner scope drains admitted child work, and finally the outer request boundary revokes the token in a finally path ahead of returning the native response. Header, body, snapshot, and upgrade operations kept past the boundary must fail with the resource-state failure, but strictly after the lifetime ends: child work consulting the token during drainage must keep succeeding. Buffered requests face revocation just as lazy ones do, and a faulted handler or a rejected route must never leave behind a usable token.
state.mandate: Can is authored by AI agents for zero external users, so past spellings and layouts carry no compatibility weight. This task terminates the server request capability after body cleanup and owner drainage. The ordering itself is already decided; advise purely on how to split the mechanism between dispatch and the server edge, plus the revoke primitive failure mode, using only the evidence supplied here. No source inspection or code execution is available to you.
state.production_paths: In production the native request is snapshotted into a frozen token, the upgrade server is attached, serveSnapshot executes within a single per-request owner scope (action matching or legacy dispatch reaching the handler), the handler result becomes a native response, any unread live body is abandoned, the scope drains, and the response goes out with server leases freed. Tests and harnesses additionally call dispatch directly with no server scope around it. A rejected route, meaning an unknown path or a disallowed method, starts no handler, hence nothing inside that scope is able to retain the token. A WebSocket upgrade seizes the native request and server during the handler, stores the socket and server object on the session instead of the token, and yields a sentinel rather than an HTTP reply. Shutdown keeps leases intact and closes exactly once; a subsequent captured-routes task inherits the dispatch boundary, so this change has to remain narrow and explicit.
state.token_mechanism: One request equals one frozen empty object indexing four WeakMaps: a read-only head-and-body snapshot, a body cell holding either buffered bytes or one live single-use wire stream, an optional upgrade-server attachment, and an upgrade-claimed set. Request abandonment merely cancels an unread live body stream while preserving every table entry, therefore buffered and lazy tokens alike remain recognized after it; a Bun 1.4.2 experiment running snapshot, abandon, and re-read back to back exhibits precisely this behavior. All header, body, snapshot, and upgrade operations look these tables up first and throw the resource-state failure on unfamiliar keys, so erasing a token from the full set of tables withdraws the complete capability in one move.
